title: Function parameters and defaults
text: A function can declare a default value for a parameter. The caller may omit that argument and Python uses the default. Default values are created when the function definition runs, so mutable defaults such as lists are shared between calls; use None and create a new object inside the function when per-call state is intended.

title: Lists
text: A list is a mutable sequence. Items can be appended, replaced, or removed after creation. Lists are useful when a collection needs to change, and their elements can be accessed by integer index.

title: Tuples and sequences
text: A tuple is an immutable sequence. Once created, its positions cannot be reassigned. A tuple can hold values of different types and is often used for a fixed group of related values. A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma.

title: Reading files with a context manager
text: Open a file with a with statement to use it as a context manager. When execution leaves the with block, the file is closed automatically, including when an exception occurs. Pass a mode such as r for reading, and specify an encoding when working with text.

title: Handling exceptions
text: Put code that may fail in a try block and handle selected error types in except blocks. Catching a specific exception makes the recovery behavior clearer. An optional else block runs when the try block finishes without an exception, and finally runs during cleanup.

title: Iterators
text: An iterator produces values one at a time. A class can support iteration by defining __iter__ to return an iterator and __next__ to return the next value. When no values remain, __next__ raises StopIteration. A generator function is a simpler way to create many iterators.

title: Modules
text: A module is a Python file whose definitions can be used from another file by importing it. Imports can name a module or selected objects. The module search path determines where Python looks for importable modules.

title: Dictionaries
text: A dictionary stores values under keys. Keys must be hashable, and looking up a value uses its key rather than a numeric position. Dictionaries can be updated by assigning a value to a key and traversed with methods such as items.
